accuracy.evidence: Checked against the National Curriculum Year 1 writing composition statement (sequencing sentences to form short narratives), Year 2 (narratives about personal experiences and those of others) and Common Core W.1.3 (two or more appropriately sequenced events, temporal words to signal event order, some sense of closure) and W.K.3 (a reaction to what happened). Every story in the lab has one valid order, time words are checked by position (First for sentence 1, Then for sentence 2, Finally for sentence 3), and each accepted ending resolves the middle's problem or gives a reaction.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented early-narrative problems: thinking order does not matter (swap prediction and the Mixed up step), time words used anywhere (prediction 'Can a story start with Finally?' and position-specific feedback), stopping with no ending (challenge 'What is missing?'), endings that restart the story or are off-topic (ending step distractors 'First, Tom went to school.' and 'The sky is blue.'), and an ending that does not match the middle (build step refuses 'I won a gold cup').

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanics are narrative sequencing itself: picture-sentence cards dragged into Beginning, Middle and End slots with a check on the order, time-word gaps filled by position, two-card swaps that repair a jumbled story, an ending choice, and a story builder where the ending must answer the chosen middle. It differs from flagoral, flagsent and flagaloud, and the 30% shingle gate passed against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child hears each card read as it lands and gets told why a wrong order fails ('Nothing can happen before it'), learns where each time word goes by trying it, repairs mixed-up stories, and in the builder discovers that a hurt-knee middle needs the plaster ending and a lost-puppy middle needs the owner ending. The step text names the idea after the task.

predictions.evidence: Two locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 'Yes, any time word works' for starting with Finally (the gap step refuses Finally in the first gap with a reason), and 'Yes, it has the same sentences' after swapping first and last (the jumbled stories read wrongly until the swap is fixed).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with twelve tagged messages: who and where put at the end or anywhere, First or Then used last, a reversed dog story judged fine or blamed on the wrong thing, a missing ending mistaken for a missing beginning or middle, a lunch ending or a restart for a lost-hat middle, and the beliefs that endings cannot hold feelings or must start with Finally.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences about a seed, a sunflower and an ice cream and pass the family limit; story cards are one short sentence each with a picture, enlarged to 14 px after the first phone screenshots. Adult text stays under grade 10 and uses the exact terms narrative, sequencing, temporal words, time connectives, story map and closure.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler patterns and the 12% duplicate gate against every lesson, including Planning Narratives, Listening to Texts Read Aloud and Saying Sentences Before Writing Them. Each kid paragraph adds one idea (three parts, order, time words, ending fits the middle); adult paragraphs cover curriculum goals, the terms, common mistakes and the lab outline.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 dark and 360 px Android light screenshots of all six steps mid-task: three story rows with wrapped sentences fit at 360 px, the First/Then/Finally tiles sit in one row, the swap highlight is clear, and full sentences also appear on large young-class buttons under the canvas; the 'Story 4 of 3' label found in screenshots was fixed.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: every task completes with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, the challenge shows, axe WCAG 2.1 AA is clean in light and dark themes, no console errors. Every drag or tap has a button carrying the full sentence (place card, take back, time words, swap card N, endings, story parts, Read my story) and the canvas aria-label reads each sentence and each result aloud.
